newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania president opens pyramid talks, refunds begin.
newsitem.headline: Albania president opens pyramid talks, refunds begin.

text.p: Rightist Albanian President Sali Berisha chaired talks on the collapse of pyramid investment schemes on Tuesday, but the main opposition group stayed away and banks prepared for the first partial refunds to distraught investors.

In Tirana's dusty streets, depositors who ploughed life savings into the schemes in Europe's poorest country gathered around newspapers reading instructions on how to recover a portion of their trapped investments later in the day.

"I have seven children. I sold my flat to put money into the schemes and now they are offering 60 percent back," said Sako Sinani, a man in his 40s. "This is robbery. This is a government of thieves."
But it was by no means certain new protests would erupt after a crackdown against demonstrators who set fire to public building last month to denounce the collapse of the schemes.
A spokeswoman said Berisha had opened round table discussions with trade unions and some parties on how to ease the effects of the failed schemes.
Opposition parties, newly united in a "Forum for Democracy", have dismissed the meeting as a publicity stunt and renewed demands for the government's resignation.
Five schemes have collapsed, but compensation has been announced for only two whose assets were frozen in state banks.
Banks were to begin allocating 60 percent of deposits to investors in one "charity foundation" known as Populli. Refunds in a second scheme were to begin on Wednesday.
Two top bankers assured depositors on television on Monday evening that they would be free to choose between cash or government certificates and could even later change their mind.

Virtually every family in the country of 3.4 million, lulled by promises of big returns, committed funds to the schemes in the six years following the fall of eastern Europe's most repressive and isolationist communist regime.

After last month's violent protests, nearly 150 people were arrested. Prosecutors are seeking long jail terms on rioting charges, prompting many would-be demonstrators to stay away from new rallies called last weekend.
For the third day running, television broadcast appeals on Monday evening to shun violence - by Moslem, Orthodox and Roman Catholic clergy.
Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi told Radio Tirana after a cabinet meeting: "The message to investors is that they should remain calm. They will get their money."
The radio announced that 24 more demonstrators had been formally charged with public offences in two southern towns.
It also said a top official in the Gjallica pyramid scheme in the south had been arrested on fraud charges.
The presiding judge in the Tirana court told local media that legal authorities were ready to start bankruptcy proceedings against Gjallica if creditors so wished.
A top leader of Berisha's Democratic Party told a visiting Italian delegation on Monday that the government's stand "was the best choice and prevented a deterioration of events".
The party, first elected in 1992, backs market reforms in the Balkan country and until last year boasted one of the best records for growth among ex-communist countries.
It won a new term last year in polls criticised as unfair and rigged by Western observers and has free rein in a parliament largely boycotted by the opposition.

The Forum for Democracy, set up last week, brings together for the first time Berisha's disparate opponents, including leftists, centrists and former political prisoners, all dedicated to ousting Prime Minister Meksi.
